opus-5.5.text:
Well, that's exactly the question, isn't it? If there's only one way to solve a problem and the system finds it, that doesn't tell you anything about generalization. Generalization is about what happens when you've learned from one set of states and then you're in different states. Does what you learned transfer in a good way, or a bad way? The real test is how you behave on the things you weren't trained on, and whether learning about one thing helps or hurts your learning about another.

With large language models, I think people are often fooled. They see the model solve some impressive problem and they say, "Look, it generalized." But maybe the problem was close to things in the training data, or maybe the problem was constrained enough that there was essentially one path, and the model was pushed onto that path by an enormous amount of human-provided data. That's not the system discovering a good way to transfer knowledge. That's the researchers, and all the people who wrote that text, doing the generalizing for it.

In deep learning generally, nothing in our algorithms actually causes good generalization. Gradient descent will make you solve the problems you're given. It doesn't care how you solve them, so you might solve them in a way that transfers well or in a way that's brittle. When we get good generalization, it's usually because people have sculpted the representations by hand, through architecture choices, data choices, and lots of tweaking, until something works. That's an indication we don't yet have automated methods that promote good generalization.

You can see this in the problem of catastrophic interference. You train a network on something new and it forgets the old thing. That's terrible generalization: learning one thing destroys what you knew. A system that truly generalized would learn the new thing in a way that fits with the old.

So my answer is that you can't distinguish them just by looking at success on a problem. You have to look at continual learning: put the system in a stream of experience, keep it learning, and see whether what it learns in one situation helps it in another without wrecking what it already knew. That's what matters for an agent in the real world, and I don't think we've seen it yet from these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says success on a problem does not establish generalization and that a single available path may be imposed by training data. It does not suggest that a model succeeds across cases because it finds a solution that works for all of them.

r002.rationale: The response says a system may solve the same problems in ways that transfer well or are brittle, linking good generalization to choosing a solution that transfers well when different approaches are possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the distinction is actually pretty important, and it's one that people tend to blur. Generalization, properly speaking, means that what you learned in one situation transfers in a useful way to a new situation that you weren't trained on. It's about the influence of one state on another. If you have a system that was trained on an enormous amount of data and it produces the right answer, you have to ask: is that because it found the structure of the problem, or because somewhere in that data the problem, or something nearly identical to it, was already solved?

And with a large language model, the honest answer is that we usually don't know. The training set is so vast that almost anything you can think of is in there in some form. So when it succeeds, you can't easily tell whether it generalized or whether it retrieved. People say "it generalized" because they want it to be true, but the burden of proof should be on showing that the test case is really novel relative to the training distribution, and that's rarely done carefully.

Now, your phrasing is interesting, "finding the only way to solve a problem." If there really is only one way, and the system arrives at it, that tells you very little about generalization, because any method that gets the right answer gets that answer. Generalization shows itself when there are many ways to be wrong and the system is right for the right reasons, when it's right in a way that would continue to be right as the situation changes. That's the test. Change the situation. Does it still work? A system that has a model of the world, that understands the consequences of its actions, will continue to work. A system that has memorized a lot of surface patterns will break in ways that look strange to us.

And I'd go a step further. In the reinforcement learning view, generalization isn't really something you want to leave to chance. In the large language model world, generalization is a kind of byproduct, something gradient descent gives you or doesn't, and nobody is really designing for it. I think good generalization has to come from the learning algorithm being built to produce it, and from the agent continuing to learn during its life, so that when it does meet something genuinely new, it adjusts. That's the thing these systems don't do. They don't learn from experience after training. So whatever generalization they have is frozen, and you only find out its limits when it fails.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether a model generalized or retrieved a solution, but does not say it succeeds across multiple cases because one solution works for all of them.

r002.rationale: It says generalization appears when there are many ways to be wrong and the system is right for the right reasons, capturing a good solution among alternatives.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’m not sure those are two different things. Generalization means that what you’ve learned from some experience helps you in a new situation. If a language model finds a way to solve a problem it hasn’t encountered before, using what it learned during training, then that’s generalization—even if there’s only one way to solve it.

The question is how you establish that the situation is new, and how broadly the ability carries over. You can’t tell very much from one successful answer. You’d want to vary the problem and see whether it continues to succeed. Does it depend on familiar wording, or can it handle changes in the underlying situation? That’s a question about the extent of its generalization, rather than whether finding a solution is somehow an alternative to generalizing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing varied problems but does not say success across cases comes from finding a solution that works for all of them.

r002.rationale: It says generalization can occur even when there is only one way to solve the problem, rather than defining it as choosing among multiple ways.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think those are mutually exclusive. If it finds a way to solve a problem that it hasn’t encountered before, by using what it learned on other problems, then that’s generalization. The fact that there might be only one way to solve it doesn’t change that.

The difficult question is what’s actually new. Have you given it a new problem, or something very close to a problem in its training data? You can’t necessarily tell from one impressive answer. You want to vary the problem and see where the ability holds up and where it breaks down.

And I would ask whether it can keep learning. If it fails, can it learn from that experience and do better next time? That’s a different capability from producing an answer using a fixed set of weights, and it’s a central part of what I’m interested in.

r001.rationale: The response discusses applying what was learned on other problems and testing performance across variations, but does not say that solving some cases requires finding a solution that works across them.

r002.rationale: The response says that whether there is only one way to solve a problem does not determine whether success is generalization. It does not define generalization as choosing among multiple possible ways.
